claims.text: Low-temperature aging of a cast or solution-treated high-entropy magnetic alloy will induce nanoscale, coherent precipitates.
Nanoscale, coherent precipitates act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning of domain walls by aging-induced precipitates increases coercive field relative to an untreated or solely solution-treated baseline.
An Fe-Co-Ni-Cr-based high-entropy magnetic alloy containing an additional precipitation-promoting element can initially lack significant nanoscale precipitates.
Aging at approximately 300–500 °C after homogenization or solution treatment can produce the proposed coercivity-enhancing microstructure.
An appropriate aging time and temperature can nucleate and grow fine, coherent precipitates without excessive coarsening or detrimental phase separation.
The coherent precipitates introduce localized increases in magnetic anisotropy.
The precipitates hinder magnetic domain-wall motion.
Hindering magnetic domain-wall motion results in a higher coercive field.
The aged alloy is expected to exhibit an approximately 20–50% increase in coercive field relative to the untreated or solely solution-treated material.
The coercivity benefit should persist only within an aging window that maintains finely dispersed, coherent precipitates.
Over-aging, precipitate coarsening, or formation of non-coherent phases may degrade coercivity.
The coercivity response depends on the specific alloy system and its susceptibility to controlled precipitation.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as aging after homogenization or solution treatment, but the permitted baseline includes an as-cast sample. An as-cast control would not be identically processed except for aging and therefore would not be a strictly matched baseline for a solution-treated-and-aged sample.
